title: How Much Does Physical Therapy Cost? 2026 Prices With and Without Insurance
summary: How much does physical therapy cost? Without insurance, about $100 to $350 per session. See evaluation prices, insurance costs, Medicare, and ways to pay less.
body_markdown:
Physical therapy is one of the most common outpatient treatments in the U.S., but what you pay depends on several factors: where you go, how many physical therapy sessions you need, and how your insurance handles them. Without insurance, a session typically costs about **$100 to $350** , and a first evaluation costs more. Here's what physical therapy costs per session and per course of care in 2026, with and without insurance, and how to estimate your own total.


## How much does physical therapy cost per session?


- **Per session without insurance:** about $100 to $350 or more, according to[Hinge Health](https://www.hingehealth.com/resources/articles/physical-therapy-cost-calculator/) , depending on the clinic, the region, and how long the visit lasts.
- **Initial evaluation without insurance:** about $150 to $400 or more (Hinge Health). At hospitals, the median self-pay price for a low-complexity evaluation is about $200 ([SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/cost/physical-therapy) ).
- **Each 15 minutes of treatment at a hospital:** the median self-pay price for one 15-minute unit of therapeutic exercise is about $93 (SelfPayRates). A typical visit includes several units.
- **With insurance:** you pay your plan's copay or coinsurance, often after meeting your deductible. Hinge Health puts typical copays at about $10 to $75 per visit.
- **Hospital vs. clinic:** hospital-based physical therapy can cost two to four times as much as an independent clinic, largely because of facility fees (Hinge Health).


These are national figures, not a quote, and your actual cost depends on your clinic and your specific plan. The rest of this guide explains what drives your physical therapy cost and how to get a real estimate before beginning treatment.


## Initial evaluation vs. follow-up physical therapy sessions


Every course of physical therapy starts with an initial evaluation, followed by shorter follow-up sessions. The evaluation usually costs more.


**The physical therapy evaluation:** at your first appointment, your physical therapist does a comprehensive assessment: reviewing your medical history, testing strength, movement, and function, setting goals, and writing an individualized treatment plan, often including a home exercise program. Evaluations are billed by complexity. At U.S. hospitals, median self-pay prices are about $200 for a low-complexity evaluation (CPT 97161), $227 for moderate complexity (97162), and $260 for high complexity (97163), according to[SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/cost/physical-therapy) .


**Follow-up sessions:** treatment visits are usually billed in 15-minute units for each type of care, such as therapeutic exercise, manual therapy, and balance training. At hospitals, the median self-pay price is about $93 to $96 per unit for each of these. A visit that includes three or four units costs a multiple of that.


## Physical therapy cost without insurance


If you're paying out of pocket, because you don't have health insurance, your plan doesn't cover physical therapy, or you've chosen an out-of-network provider, you'll pay the physical therapy clinic's self-pay rate. Many clinics have set prices for cash patients.


- **Independent clinics:** often the lower-cost option. Hinge Health estimates a 12-session course at an independent clinic at about $1,200 to $2,400.
- **Hospital outpatient departments:** the same 12 sessions at a hospital facility cost about $2,400 to $4,200 (Hinge Health).
- **Hospital self-pay prices vary by state:** the median price for a 15-minute therapeutic exercise unit ranges from about $37 in New Jersey to about $171 in Arizona ([SelfPayRates](https://selfpayrates.com/cost/physical-therapy) ).


Ask any clinic for its cash price before your first appointment. Some offer a lower rate for paying at the time of service or for buying a package of visits.


If you have a high deductible, it's worth comparing the clinic's cash price with your plan's allowed amount. Paying cash may cost less than paying the full allowed amount before your deductible is met, but payments made outside your insurance may not count toward your deductible.


## Physical therapy cost with insurance coverage


Most health insurance plans cover medically necessary outpatient physical therapy, but your out-of-pocket cost depends on your plan design and your insurance benefits:


- **Deductible:** until you meet your[deductible](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) , you usually pay the full allowed amount for each visit.
- **Copay:** a fixed amount per visit, such as $30. See[how copays work](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-copay) .
- **Coinsurance:** a percentage of the allowed amount. If your plan allows $150 for a visit and your[coinsurance](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) is 20%, you pay $30.
- **Visit limits:** many plans cap the number of physical therapy visits per year or require prior authorization after a set number of sessions.
- **Network status:** in-network physical therapists charge your plan's negotiated rate. Out-of-network care may have a separate deductible, higher coinsurance, or no coverage at all. See[in-network vs. out-of-network](https://www.withflex.com/blog/in-network-vs-out-of-network) .


Once you reach your plan's[out-of-pocket maximum](https://www.withflex.com/blog/deductible-vs-out-of-pocket-maximum) , your plan pays for covered care for the rest of the plan year.


**Questions to ask your insurance company or insurance provider before you start:**


- What is my copay or coinsurance for outpatient physical therapy?
- How much of my deductible have I met?
- Is this clinic in network?
- How many visits are covered per year?
- Do I need a referral or prior authorization?


## How setting and location change the cost of physical therapy


Where you get care often affects the price more than which body part is being treated.


- **Independent or private practice clinics** are usually the most affordable setting for the same treatment.
- **Hospital-based PT** often adds a facility fee on top of the therapist's charges, which is why it can cost two to four times as much.
- **Home visits** can cost more per visit because of the therapist's travel time, though they save you the trip.
- **Location** matters too: as the state figures above show, the same 15 minutes of hospital-based therapy can cost several times as much in one state as in another.


If your doctor refers you to a hospital-based program and cost is a concern, ask whether an in-network independent clinic would work for your treatment.


## What goes into a physical therapy bill


- **Session length:** appointments often run 30 to 60 minutes. Longer visits usually mean more billable units.
- **Treatment types:** therapeutic exercise, hands-on manual therapy, neuromuscular re-education, balance training, and modalities such as electrical stimulation. Each is billed with its own CPT code.
- **Billing units:** most outpatient physical therapy is billed in 15-minute units, so a 45-minute visit might include three units across different codes.
- **Specialty care:** clinics that focus on areas such as pelvic health, vestibular rehab, or sports injuries, where therapists have advanced training, may charge more per session.


Ask the clinic how long visits last, how many units a typical visit is billed for, and how much of the visit is one-on-one with the physical therapist.


## How many sessions will you need?


Your total cost is roughly the price per session times the number of sessions. That number depends on your condition, whether it is acute or chronic, whether you're recovering from surgery, and how consistently you do your home exercises. A minor sprain may need only a few visits, while post-surgical rehabilitation after a joint replacement or ligament surgery often takes months of multiple sessions per week.


Your physical therapist will estimate the number of visits at your initial evaluation. Ask for the plan in writing, including how often you'll come in and for how long, and use it to estimate your total:


- **Example 1:** 6 visits at a $150 cash rate = $900.
- **Example 2:** 12 visits with a $40 copay = $480, if your plan covers all 12.


These examples are for illustration only; use your clinic's prices and your plan's cost-sharing to estimate your overall cost.


## Medicare Part B and physical therapy costs in 2026


Medicare Part B helps pay for medically necessary outpatient physical therapy. After you meet the Part B deductible, which is[$283 in 2026](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/2026-medicare-parts-b-premiums-deductibles) , you generally pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, according to[Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/physical-therapy-services) .


- **No hard cap:** there's no limit on how much Medicare pays for medically necessary outpatient therapy in a year (Medicare.gov).
- **Threshold for documentation:** once your physical therapy and speech-language pathology costs pass $2,480 in 2026, your therapist must confirm on the claim that continued care is medically necessary ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/therapy-services) ).
- **Medicare Advantage:** these plans set their own copays, networks, and prior authorization rules, so check your plan.


## Direct access: do you need a referral?


Direct access means you can see a physical therapist without a referral from a doctor first. Patients in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and the U.S. Virgin Islands now have some form of direct access, according to the[American Physical Therapy Association (APTA)](https://www.apta.org/advocacy/issues/direct-access-advocacy) . Direct access laws differ by state, and in many states that access comes with limits, such as a cap on visits or days before a physician must be involved.


Skipping a visit to another healthcare provider for a referral can save time and money. But your insurance plan may still require a referral or prior authorization to cover physical therapy, even when state law doesn't, so check both.


## Ways to lower your PT costs


- **Choose an in-network, non-hospital clinic** when it fits your treatment.
- **Ask for self-pay rates** if you're uninsured or haven't met a high deductible.
- **Do your prescribed exercises.** Keeping up with at-home exercises can help you progress, which may let you taper to fewer sessions sooner. Ask your therapist.
- **Ask about telehealth visits** for check-ins and exercise progressions.
- **Ask about digital physical therapy programs** your employer or health plan may offer.
- **Ask about payment plans** if you need to spread the cost over time.


Whether you can pay with health savings accounts (HSAs) or flexible spending accounts (FSAs) depends on your plan, and[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) describes which medical expenses qualify. Our guide to[HSAs and FSAs](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) explains how the two accounts work.
